messages.body_plain:
Hello Simone -

There is not a single edgewise shared partner number for a network; it 
is a distribution. In your network below, there are three edges, and 
each has one shared partner.  The edgewise shared partner distribution 
for the network would then be

0 edges with 0 SPs
3 edges with 1 SP
0 edges with 2 SPs
0 edges wtth 3 SPs
etc.

Imagine if in addition to the three edges you listed, there were also 
a--d and d--b. The distribution would then be:

0 edges with 0 SPs
4 edges with 1 SP
1 edge with 2 SPs
0 edges with 3 SPs
etc.

Hope that helps,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
On 04/05/2014 05:15 PM, Jesse Sayles wrote:
> Does anyone know how I can print the name of a given node / vertex using
> the network or sna package?

Assuming you have previously set the vertex names, you can get them with

network.vertex.names(myNetwork)

you can also set them with

network.vertex.names(myNetwork)<-myVectorOfNames

since vertex names are essentially an ordinary attribute you can also 
get and set them with the regular attribute tools.

get.vertex.attribute(myNetwork,'vertex.names')


If you are working in a dynamic case, and are using the names as unique 
identifiers for the vertices, you may want to check out the Persistent 
IDs functionality in the networkDynamic package for translating between 
the ids and network ids

?persistent.ids

best,
  -skye

messages.body_plain:
I would like to see the network package API evolve towards more consistent treatment of the %e% operator.

The usage of the %e% operator is confusing because as a setter it takes one type of object (a matrix) and as a getter it returns a different one (a list). My students have a lot of trouble with this. I can't think of another programming language where the result of a 'get' operation is not a valid argument to the 'set' operation.

Example:

# create simple network
n <- network.initialize(5)
n[1,] <- 1
n[2,3] <- 1
n[,5] <- 1

# set the bar attribute
set.edge.attribute(n, "bar", 1:8)
set.vertex.attribute(n, "baz", 1:5)

# naively set the foo attribute to be the "same" as the bar attribute
n %e% "foo" <- n %e% "bar"

# different assignment of attributes
as.sociomatrix(n, attrname="bar")
as.sociomatrix(n, attrname="foo")

I know this is "just how it works" and probably there is a lot of legacy code that depends on this idiosyncratic behavior. Still, I would suggest that the developers consider changing %e% (and I guess get.edge.value as well) to return a matrix value, so that the API is consistent. get.edge.attribute would still be there as the way to get a list of the attribute values.

__________________________________________________________
Robin Burke, Professor
College of Computing and Digital Media, DePaul University
rburke@cdm.depaul.edu

struggling with a theoretical issue for a few months now and I'm hoping

status is at least partially endogenously determined by the network

in the sense that one's sex, race or height is the same when the network is
just forming as it is once it has reached its observable state. In the
stergm framework, node-level attributes are also fixed across time.

How might one address node-level attributes that are known to have changed
over time? These attributes may be either historically observable are known
to accumulate endogenously as in the case of eigenvector centrality.

Thanks in advance for your help!

Jameson

Not so noob-ish, actually.  This is a good question.

At this point the statnet tools implement ergms for edge changes only. 
The vertex attributes are assumed fixed (or, in stergm, changing due to an 
exogenous process, like demographics, that you would need to program 
separately).

We are working on developing the theory/code for ergms with joint 
vertex/edge dynamics.  For estimation from cross-sectional data Ian 
Fellows has done quite a bit of work, so you might correspond with him 
<ian@fellstat.com>.  For estimation from longitudinal data, we have a 
dissertation in progress.

RSiena has the capability to model joint vertex/edge dynamics now.  So 
your best bet for now may be to work with that.

best,
Martina

This problem showed up when my students were attempting to compute Bonacich centrality on a network converted from directed.

See the code below:

library(igraph)
library(network)
library(intergraph)
library(sna)

net <- network.initialize(5)

net[1,2] <- 1
net[2,3] <- 1
net[2,4] <- 1
net[2,5] <- 1
net[5,1] <- 1

undir <- as.network(net, directed=FALSE)
undir2 <- asNetwork(as.undirected(asIgraph(net)))

as.matrix(net)
as.matrix(undir)
as.matrix(undir2)

bonpow(undir) # Generates an error
bonpow(undir2) # Computes correct result

I realize that you can guarantee this via symmetrize but it seems to me that as.matrix should return a symmetric matrix when the network is undirected. Is there an option I?m missing (either to as.network or as.matrix) to guarantee this?

Hi, Robin.  The reason that you are getting a directed adjacency matrix 
is that undir here is not undirected.  (You can verify that with 
is.directed(undir).)  This is because you started out by creating a 
directed network object (net), and did not at any point symmetrize it; 
you seem to be trying to use as.network to do this, and that's not how 
that function works.  In particular, as.network will coerce its first 
argument to a network object, only invoking subsequent arguments if 
necessary to perform construction - if you pass it a network object, it 
will just return that object.  So this is not an error - that's what the 
function is supposed to do.

One could consider altering the functionality of as.network and friends 
to perform additional coercion, although this raises the usual issue 
that one would have to have a clear way of performing said coercion for 
all cases.  (This is not always trivial, particularly when you consider 
that network objects can be multiplex, carry complex attributes, etc.)  
If there's demand for that, it's something we might consider adding to 
future releases. In the interim, though, you should not assume that 
as.network and friends can be used to alter existing network objects.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Dear statnet community and developers,

I have been playing around with the simulate.ergm and simulate.formula 
functions lately. I don't really understand why they produce different 
results in some cases. It would be very helpful for me if somebody could 
comment on the following simulation experiment to help me understand how 
they work:

##########

library("statnet")
nw <- network(matrix(rbinom(10000, 1, 0.01), nrow = 100))
fit <- ergm(nw ~ edges)

# experiment 1:
sim1 <- simulate.formula(nw ~ edges, nsim = 500, coef = coef(fit))
mat1 <- as.matrix(sim1[[1]])
for (i in 2:500) {
   mat1 <- mat1 + as.matrix(sim1[[i]])
}

# experiment 2:
sim2 <- simulate.ergm(fit, nsim = 500)
mat2 <- as.matrix(sim2[[1]])
for (i in 2:500) {
   mat2 <- mat2 + as.matrix(sim2[[i]])
}

# plot the results of the two experiments:
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(table(mat1), main = "simulate.formula")
barplot(table(mat2), main = "simulate.ergm")

##########

First, I create a fairly sparse toy network with 100 nodes and fit a 
simple model to the network which only contains an edges term. Then I 
simulate 500 new networks from this model, once using simulate.ergm and 
once using simulate.formula. I add up the 500 network matrices in each 
case. Since I only used an edges term, I would expect to find 
approximately the same frequency in each cell of the matrix, with some 
random variation. However, if I look at the frequency distributions of 
the two aggregated matrices, these distributions look somewhat different 
(see the barplots). One of them has the expected bell curve while the 
other one seems to be substantially right-skewed. (Note: the whole code 
takes about five minutes to complete on a recent desktop computer.) What 
is the explanation of this difference? Shouldn't this affect my 
goodness-of-fit assessment if I mistakenly choose the wrong function to 
simulate new networks?

Thanks and best regards

Philip

messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip -

Thanks for your detailed example - it makes recreating straightforward, 
and helped me dramatically with the diagnosing.

It seems to be an issue of different default values for one of the 
control parameters between the two routines.  Specifically, 
simulate.formula invokes control.simulate.formula, which defaults to an 
interval of 1000 MCMC steps between draws in the simulation (via the 
argument MCMC.interval).  For simulate.ergm, it's only 100.  That means 
that by default simulate.ergm won't move as far away on average in 
consecutive draws, and there will be more auto-correlation between two 
consecutive draws for larger networks, as you saw in your plots.

Of course, the user always has the option to change these control 
parameters instead of accepting the default, but we recognize there are 
many such parameters and it's not practical to assume that every user 
will explore all of these all of the time.  I'll add a ticket now to 
standardize these for the next release.

Yours,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Philip.  In response to your three questions, 

(1) Autocorrelation is not a bad thing per se.  There is a tradeoff in MCMC between storage and information:  Ideally, one should keep every single iteration because even highly correlated values provide some additional information about parameters.  However, in the ERGM context we don?t do this because the storage-cost-to-information ratio is too high.  This is not to say, though, that autocorrelation should be eliminated entirely, as the resulting loss of information and therefore efficiency might be too great?plus, it?s generally impossible to eliminate autocorrelation entirely and so one would have to implement some kind of (necessarily ad hoc) scheme to try to check for autocorrelation.  Bottom line, it?s not an exact science and ?accidental misinterpretation? is not necessarily caused by autocorrelation.

(2) In light of (1), I don?t think ?required MCMC interval? has any meaning.  That said, trying to find good (i.e., effective) default values is an interesting theoretical question, though from a practical point of view it may not be worth a great deal of effort to try to solve.  Also note that there is a huge literature on MCMC routines that attempts to answer roughly this same question, and for every effective-looking rule of thumb, there?s always a pathological counterexample on which it fails utterly.

(3) Good point.  Perhaps we should point out that when these control values are null, the value that?s used is the one contained in the ergm object itself (in object$control).  As this value comes from the control.ergm function by default, you?ll find this value in the help for control.ergm.

Hope this is helpful (and that my answers to (1) and (2) don?t sound flippant; they?re not intended to be!)
Dave
